gloss_readable: This term refers to a physical blemish or defect that disqualifies someone from service. In Daniel 1:4, it describes the requirement that young men chosen for the king's court be without any physical imperfection. The cross-linguistic evidence (Spanish defecto, French défaut) emphasizes the notion of a flaw or imperfection, whether visible or hidden, that would make someone unsuitable for select service.

senses.1: Physical blemish or bodily defect. The qere reading and multilingual glosses (blemish, defecto, défaut) converge on the idea of a disqualifying physical imperfection. Daniel 1:4 specifies that candidates for royal service must be free from such defects, highlighting ancient standards of physical perfection for court positions.

gloss_terse: refuse, offscouring, that which is rejected or despised
gloss_readable: A rare term meaning refuse or offscouring, appearing only in Lamentations 3:45. BDB defines it as something rejected or cast away. The word appears in a context where Jerusalem describes itself as scum and refuse among the nations—a powerful image of degradation and rejection. The multilingual evidence shows variations in how languages handle this rare term, with some simply transliterating it.

senses.1: Refuse, offscouring, rejected waste. BDB translates the phrase as 'offscouring and refuse thou makest us,' depicting Israel's humiliation. The English gloss 'refuse' and Spanish 'rechazo' (rejection) capture the sense of something utterly cast away. Lamentations 3:45 uses this alongside another word for scum to intensify the image of national degradation.

gloss_terse: den, light-hole, opening in a serpent's lair
gloss_readable: A hapax legomenon denoting the den or light-hole of a serpent. In Isaiah 11:8, it appears in a messianic vision where a child plays near the den of a venomous snake without harm. BDB notes debate over whether this means the snake's den or its eye-ball, though the den interpretation is more widely accepted. The term evokes the dangerous dwelling place that will become safe in the age to come.

senses.1: Den or light-hole of a serpent. Isaiah 11:8 places this in an eschatological context where predators and prey coexist peacefully. The multilingual glosses (den-of, cueva-de) support the interpretation of a serpent's lair. BDB mentions an alternative reading of 'eye-ball' based on Targumic tradition, but the den reading better fits the parallel structure with other animal habitats in the passage.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic term for balances or scales, appearing in the dramatic scene of Daniel 5:27. The word is part of the divine judgment pronounced at Belshazzar's feast: 'You have been weighed in the balances and found wanting.' The image of weighing emphasizes divine measurement and moral assessment. Cross-linguistic glosses consistently render this as balance or scales, preserving the metaphor of divine judgment.

senses.1: Balances, weighing scales used metaphorically for divine judgment. Daniel 5:27 uses this as part of the interpretation of the writing on the wall, where God has weighed the Babylonian king and found him deficient. The multilingual evidence (balances, balanza, balance) maintains the image of precise measurement, underscoring that God's assessment is exact and inescapable.

gloss_terse: exertions, mighty efforts, displays of strength
gloss_readable: A plural construct form meaning exertions or displays of power and strength. Appearing only in Job 36:19, the term is part of Elihu's speech questioning whether wealth or mighty efforts can deliver someone from distress. BDB defines it as power, strength, or force exerted. The phrase 'exertions of strength' suggests straining or maximum effort that ultimately proves insufficient apart from God.

senses.1: Exertions of power, mighty efforts or displays of strength. Job 36:19 uses this in parallel with wealth to ask whether either can rescue someone in trouble. The English 'exertions-of' captures the sense of strenuous effort, while the context suggests these human resources are inadequate. The term emphasizes the futility of relying on human strength when facing divine discipline.

gloss_terse: refusing, those who refuse to obey
gloss_readable: An adjectival form describing those who refuse or are disobedient. Jeremiah 13:10 uses this to characterize an evil people who refuse to hear God's words. The term is formed from the root meaning 'to refuse' and appears with the definite article as a substantive, identifying a class of people marked by stubborn resistance to divine instruction. The multilingual evidence consistently captures the idea of refusal or rejection.

senses.1: The refusing ones, those characterized by disobedience and refusal to listen. Jeremiah 13:10 applies this to people who stubbornly refuse to hear God's words, walk in their own stubborn hearts, and follow other gods. The Spanish 'los-que-rehúsan' (those who refuse) precisely captures this substantival use. The context links refusal to hear with fundamental spiritual rebellion.

gloss_terse: thing baked, baked goods from an oven
gloss_readable: A term for something baked, specifically referring to baked goods prepared in an oven. In Leviticus 2:4, it appears in instructions for grain offerings baked in an oven. The term emphasizes the method of preparation—oven-baking—as distinct from other cooking methods mentioned in the sacrificial regulations. Cross-linguistic evidence consistently renders this as related to baking or cooking.

senses.1: A baking, something baked in an oven. Leviticus 2:4 uses this in the phrase 'a grain offering, a baking of an oven,' specifying one acceptable method of preparation for offerings. The multilingual glosses (baking-of, cocido-de, cuisson-de) all emphasize the baking process. This technical culinary-liturgical term distinguishes oven-baked offerings from those prepared on griddles or in pans.

gloss_readable: A word for darkness, appearing in Joshua 24:7 in the account of the Exodus. God placed darkness between the Israelites and the Egyptians at the Red Sea, providing cover and separation. This darkness was both protective for Israel and terrifying for Egypt. The multilingual glosses unanimously render this as darkness, obscurity, or gloom, capturing the sense of impenetrable blackness that served as divine intervention.

senses.1: Darkness, deep gloom placed as a barrier. Joshua 24:7 recalls how God 'set darkness between you and the Egyptians' during the exodus. The cross-linguistic evidence (darkness, oscuridad, ténèbres, Finsternis) consistently points to thick darkness. This supernatural darkness served a dual purpose: protecting Israel while confounding Egypt, demonstrating God's control over natural elements for his people's deliverance.

gloss_terse: thick darkness, deep gloom, utter obscurity
gloss_readable: A rare intensified form meaning thick or deep darkness, appearing only in Jeremiah 2:31. The term is enhanced with a suffix suggesting extreme darkness or gloom. Jeremiah uses this metaphorically, asking whether God has been like a land of thick darkness to his people. The rhetorical question expects a negative answer—God has not been dark or obscure, yet his people have wandered away. BDB notes scholarly debate about the precise morphology.

senses.1: Thick darkness, deep gloom used figuratively. Jeremiah 2:31 asks, 'Have I been a land of thick darkness to Israel?' implying God has been light and provision, not obscurity. The Spanish gloss 'densa-oscuridad' (dense darkness) captures the intensified sense. The parallel with 'wilderness' suggests inhospitable, frightening terrain, making the rhetorical force stronger: God has been anything but dark to his people.

gloss_readable: A participial form meaning separated or set apart, describing cities in Joshua 16:9. The term likely refers to cities designated for the tribe of Ephraim that were separated out from the territory of Manasseh. BDB suggests textual emendation to a Hophal or Niphal participle, indicating these were 'separated cities.' The multilingual evidence reflects this sense of separation or distinction.

senses.1: The separated ones, cities set apart or distinguished. Joshua 16:9 mentions 'the separated cities' allotted to Ephraim within Manasseh's inheritance. The Spanish 'las-separadas' and English 'the-separated' support this reading. BDB's suggestion of a passive participle ('cities that were separated') fits the context of tribal boundary descriptions where some cities were set apart for one tribe within another's borders.

gloss_readable: A plural construct form meaning entrances or gateways, used in Ezekiel 27:3. The term appears in a lament over Tyre, describing the city as dwelling 'at the entrances of the sea.' This geographic description emphasizes Tyre's strategic position as a maritime trading hub with access to multiple sea routes. The word conveys both physical gateways and metaphorical points of entry to commercial networks.

senses.1: Entrances, gateways to the sea. Ezekiel 27:3 uses this to characterize Tyre's advantageous coastal position: 'dwelling at the entrances of the sea, merchant of peoples for many coastlands.' The multilingual glosses (entrances-of, las-entradas-de, entrée) consistently render this as entry points or gates. The maritime context makes this about harbor access and sea-lane control, essential to Tyre's commercial dominance.

gloss_readable: A term denoting emptiness or void, appearing in Nahum 2:10 in a triplet of devastation words: 'Desolation, and void, and waste.' This is part of a prophetic description of Nineveh's coming destruction. The three synonyms intensify the image of total ruin. The word emphasizes the vacant, empty state that follows plundering and destruction. Cross-linguistic renderings capture the sense of emptiness and desolation.

senses.1: Void, emptiness resulting from devastation. Nahum 2:10 uses this in a powerful threefold description of Nineveh's fate. The Spanish 'y-vaciada' (emptied out) and French 'et-vide' (and void) emphasize the state of being drained or depleted. The triplet structure ('desolation, void, waste') creates a rhythmic intensification, hammering home the completeness of Nineveh's coming judgment.

gloss_terse: choice, select, the best or finest
gloss_readable: A noun meaning choice or select, likely a scribal variant of the more common word for 'choicest.' In 2 Kings 3:19, it describes 'every choice city' that Israel would strike during their campaign against Moab. The term emphasizes quality and desirability—the best cities, not just any settlement. BDB notes this is probably a scribal error for the standard form, but the meaning remains clear: the finest or most valuable.

senses.1: Choice, select, the finest or best. 2 Kings 3:19 uses this in the phrase 'every choice city,' referring to the prime settlements of Moab targeted for destruction. The multilingual glosses (choice, escogida) consistently render this as select or chosen. Though BDB suggests a scribal variant, the context of military campaign makes the sense clear: Israel would strike Moab's best fortified and most valuable cities.

gloss_readable: A personal name meaning 'choice' or 'select,' belonging to one of David's mighty warriors in 1 Chronicles 11:38. The name derives from the root meaning 'to choose,' suggesting the bearer was chosen or select. This warrior is listed among David's elite fighting men, and his name fittingly means 'choice'—an apt designation for someone in this distinguished group.

senses.1: Mibhar, proper name of one of David's warriors. The name means 'choice' or 'select,' from the root 'to choose.' 1 Chronicles 11:38 lists him among the mighty men who supported David. The multilingual evidence shows transliteration (Mibjar, Mivchar), preserving the Hebrew name. His inclusion in this elite roster of warriors makes the name particularly appropriate.

gloss_readable: A rare word meaning source of comfort or brightening, appearing only in Jeremiah 8:18. The prophet laments, 'My source of comfort in sorrow.' BDB translates this as 'a source of brightening to me in sorrow,' suggesting something that brings light or cheer amid grief. The text is marked as dubious by scholars, but the general sense of consolation amid distress is clear. The term emphasizes the prophet's deep need for comfort in the face of his people's judgment.

senses.1: Source of comfort or brightening amid sorrow. Jeremiah 8:18 expresses the prophet's anguish: 'My source of comfort in grief.' BDB suggests this means something that brightens or cheers, bringing light into darkness. The Spanish 'Mi-consuelo' (my consolation) captures the personal, possessive sense. Though the text is questioned by some scholars, Jeremiah's emotional state—seeking comfort while pronouncing judgment—is poignantly conveyed.

gloss_readable: A term for structure or building, appearing in Ezekiel 40:2 in the prophet's temple vision. Ezekiel sees a structure 'like the structure of a city' on a high mountain. The word emphasizes the architectural dimension—not just a building but a carefully designed structure. The visionary temple Ezekiel sees is vast and complex, compared to an entire city's layout. The term highlights the organized, planned nature of what the prophet witnesses.

senses.1: Structure, building, architectural construction. Ezekiel 40:2 uses this in the phrase 'like the structure of a city,' describing the visionary temple's scale and complexity. The multilingual glosses (structure-of, edificio-de, édifice) consistently render this as a built edifice. The comparison to a city emphasizes the temple's grandeur—not a simple building but an elaborate complex requiring detailed description through the following chapters.

gloss_terse: Mebunnai, personal name of one of David's heroes
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing in 2 Samuel 23:27, identifying one of David's thirty mighty men. Scholars note this is likely a textual corruption, and the parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 11:29 reads Sibbecai instead. This kind of textual variation between Samuel and Chronicles is not uncommon due to scribal transmission. The name appears in the roster of David's elite warriors who accomplished extraordinary military feats.

senses.1: Mebunnai, proper name of one of David's mighty men. 2 Samuel 23:27 lists him among the thirty heroes, though the parallel in 1 Chronicles 11:29 reads Sibbecai, which most scholars prefer. BDB suggests this is a scribal error. The multilingual evidence shows transliteration (Mevunay, Mebunnai), treating it as a proper name. Despite the textual question, he belongs to David's elite warrior class.

gloss_readable: A plural noun meaning genitals or private parts that excite shame. The term appears in Deuteronomy 25:11 in a law addressing a woman who intervenes in a fight between her husband and another man by seizing the other man's genitals. This is treated as a serious offense requiring corporal punishment. The euphemistic Hebrew emphasizes the shameful or private nature of these body parts. Cross-linguistic glosses handle this with varying degrees of directness.

senses.1: Genitals, private parts, pudenda. Deuteronomy 25:11 legislates a case where a woman grabs a man's genitals during a fight. BDB notes these are 'parts that excite shame,' reflecting ancient modesty around sexual organs. The multilingual evidence ranges from direct (genitals) to euphemistic (partes-vergonzosas, shameful parts). The law's severity suggests this was considered a grave violation of propriety and dignity.

gloss_readable: A plural noun meaning cooking-places or kitchens, appearing in Ezekiel 46:23. The prophet's temple vision includes detailed descriptions of various rooms and their functions, including designated areas for cooking sacrificial portions. The term is parallel to 'house of the boilers' in the following verse, confirming this refers to cooking facilities. These kitchens were necessary infrastructure for processing sacrifices in the temple complex.

senses.1: Cooking-places, kitchens for boiling. Ezekiel 46:23 describes architectural features in the temple vision, specifying areas designated for cooking. The parallel in verse 24, 'house of the boilers,' confirms this function. The multilingual glosses (boiling-places, cocinas, lieu-de-cuisine) consistently identify these as kitchen or cooking facilities. The temple's elaborate design included practical spaces for preparing sacrificial meals.

gloss_terse: Magbish, family name or place name
gloss_readable: A name appearing in Ezra 2:30, identifying either a family or place associated with returning exiles: 'sons of Magbish.' Interestingly, this name is omitted in the parallel list in Nehemiah 7:33, though Greek manuscripts include it. Scholars debate whether this refers to a family name or a place from which exiles returned. The LXX preserves various forms of the name, showing it was recognized in ancient translations despite the Nehemiah omission.

senses.1: Magbish, name of a family or place of returning exiles. Ezra 2:30 lists 'sons of Magbish' among those returning from Babylonian exile. The parallel passage in Nehemiah 7:33 omits this, though Greek manuscripts include it. BDB notes the variants in LXX (Magebos, Magbeis), showing textual diversity. Whether a family name or hometown, it identifies a group participating in the return from exile.

gloss_readable: A plural noun meaning twisted things or braided cords, appearing in Exodus 28:14. The term describes decorative chains for the high priest's breastplate, made of pure gold and woven into braided cords. These chains attached the breastplate to the ephod. The word emphasizes the twisted or braided nature of the workmanship. The multilingual evidence consistently renders this as twisted, braided, or corded, highlighting the intricate craftsmanship.

senses.1: Twisted cords, braided chains of gold. Exodus 28:14 specifies these as part of the high priest's vestments: 'chains of pure gold, twisted.' The term appears in apposition to 'braided chains,' clarifying the twisting technique. The multilingual glosses (twisted, trenzadas, retors, gezwirnt) all emphasize the braided or twisted nature. This describes specialized metalwork creating decorative and functional fasteners for sacred garments.

gloss_terse: Migdal-El, place name meaning 'tower of God'
gloss_readable: A place name meaning 'tower of God,' located in the territory of Naphtali according to Joshua 19:38. This fortified town may be the same as Magdala mentioned in Matthew 15:39, identified with Mejdel in the plain of Gennesareth. The name suggests a prominent structure—either a watchtower or fortress—associated with divine protection or dedication. Such towers served both military and symbolic functions in ancient settlements.

senses.1: Migdal-El, place name meaning 'tower of God' in Naphtali. Joshua 19:38 lists this among Naphtali's fortified cities. BDB suggests identification with Magdala of the Gospels and modern Mejdel near the Sea of Galilee. The name components ('tower' + 'God') suggest a fortress or watchtower with religious significance. The multilingual evidence shows transliteration (Migdal-el, Migdal-El), preserving the Hebrew compound name.

gloss_terse: Migdal-Gad, place name meaning 'tower of Gad'
gloss_readable: A place name meaning 'tower of Gad,' located in the territory of Judah according to Joshua 15:37. Scholars have proposed identification with Mejdel east of Ashkelon, though this remains uncertain. The name suggests either a tower dedicated to the god Gad, or more likely a watchtower associated with the Israelite tribe of Gad. Like other 'Migdal' compounds, this indicates a fortified position or prominent tower in Judah's Shephelah region.

senses.1: Migdal-Gad, place name meaning 'tower of Gad' in Judah. Joshua 15:37 lists this among cities in Judah's lowlands. BDB suggests possible identification with Mejdel east of Ashkelon. The name combines 'tower' with 'Gad' (either the deity or tribe), suggesting a fortified site. The multilingual evidence shows transliteration (Migdal-Gad), preserving the compound. This was one of several 'tower' place names marking strategic positions.

gloss_terse: Migdal-Eder, place name meaning 'tower of the flock'
gloss_readable: A place name meaning 'tower of the flock' or 'watchtower of the herd,' appearing in Genesis 35:21 and Micah 4:8. This was a shepherd's watchtower near Bethlehem where Jacob camped. Such towers allowed shepherds to watch over their flocks and detect approaching predators or thieves. Micah uses this name metaphorically for Jerusalem, calling it the 'tower of the flock,' emphasizing God's watchful care over his people.

senses.1: Migdal-Eder, place name meaning 'tower of the flock,' a shepherd's watchtower near Bethlehem. Genesis 35:21 locates Jacob's camp here. The name describes a tower's function: watching over flocks. Micah 4:8 uses this metaphorically for Jerusalem: 'tower of the flock, stronghold of daughter Zion.' The multilingual evidence shows transliteration (Migdal-Eder), preserving the Hebrew. This pastoral image conveys both practical security and theological care.

gloss_readable: A term for an axe or cutting instrument, appearing in 2 Samuel 12:31. David put captured Ammonites to forced labor 'at the saws and at the iron axes.' This describes harsh treatment of prisoners of war, setting them to brutal construction or demolition work. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 20:3 confirms this reading. The multilingual evidence shows some variation in rendering this compound phrase involving axes and other tools.

senses.1: Axe, iron cutting instrument used in forced labor. 2 Samuel 12:31 describes David putting Ammonite captives to work with saws and iron axes, likely in quarrying or demolition. The term emphasizes the cutting function of this implement. Some translations struggle with the prepositional phrase, rendering it variously as 'at axes' or 'with axes.' The parallel in Chronicles confirms these were iron tools for harsh labor.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic word meaning scroll or book-roll, appearing in Ezra 6:2. During the search for Cyrus's decree authorizing temple rebuilding, a scroll was found in the citadel at Ecbatana. This refers to the physical format of ancient documents—leather or papyrus sheets rolled around a rod. The discovery of this scroll provided legal proof of Persian authorization for the temple project. The term is the Aramaic equivalent of the Hebrew word for scroll.

senses.1: Scroll, book-roll containing a written decree. Ezra 6:2 reports finding 'a scroll' with Cyrus's authorization for rebuilding the temple. This Aramaic term matches the Hebrew 'megillah,' both referring to rolled documents. The multilingual evidence (scroll, rollo, Rolle) consistently renders this as a rolled document. The discovery of this archival scroll vindicated the Jews' claim to Persian support for their temple project.

gloss_readable: A hapax legomenon of uncertain meaning in Habakkuk 1:9, describing the Chaldean invaders. The text reads literally 'the eagerness of their faces is eastward' or 'forward.' Scholars debate whether this means eager determination, the assembling or massing of their forces, or simply their forward motion. BDB notes the text is probably corrupt. Nevertheless, the context describes the unstoppable advance of the Babylonian army, and this term somehow characterizes their relentless forward momentum.

senses.1: Eagerness, forward intent, or direction of advance. Habakkuk 1:9 uses this of the Chaldeans: 'the eagerness of their faces forward.' BDB suggests meanings ranging from 'assembling' to 'eagerness,' comparing questionable Arabic cognates. The Spanish gloss 'la-dirección-de' (the direction of) reflects uncertainty. Despite textual difficulties, the context of Babylonian invasion makes clear this describes their focused, relentless advance toward conquest.

gloss_terse: covering, hardness of heart, spiritual obstinacy
gloss_readable: A rare word meaning covering, appearing in Lamentations 3:65 as 'covering of heart.' This describes spiritual hardness or obstinacy—a shell or veil over the heart preventing understanding. Some interpret this as obstinacy or stubbornness, others as blindness of heart. The image is of something that shields or covers the heart, preventing God's word from penetrating. The Quranic parallel cited in BDB shows similar imagery of covers placed on hearts to prevent belief.

senses.1: Covering of heart, hardness or blindness preventing spiritual understanding. Lamentations 3:65 asks God to give enemies 'covering of heart'—either obstinacy or blindness. BDB compares Quranic imagery of coverings on hearts preventing belief. The Spanish 'dureza-de' (hardness of) captures the sense of impenetrability. This describes a judicial hardening where God gives people over to their chosen spiritual blindness.

gloss_readable: A term for rebuke or reproof, appearing in Deuteronomy 28:20 among covenant curses. God threatens to send 'rebuke' upon disobedient Israel along with confusion and frustration. This rebuke is more than verbal correction—it represents God's active opposition and judgment against covenant-breakers. The term carries weight of divine displeasure and punitive action. The multilingual evidence consistently renders this as rebuke or reproof, though some show the threatening dimension.

senses.1: Rebuke, stern reproof expressing divine judgment. Deuteronomy 28:20 lists this among curses for covenant disobedience: 'YHWH will send upon you cursing, confusion, and rebuke.' The Spanish 'la-amenaza' (the threat) captures the menacing aspect beyond mere verbal correction. This rebuke accompanies divine action against rebels—not just words but active judgment demonstrating God's displeasure with covenant violation.

gloss_terse: Magpiash, personal name of a leader who sealed the covenant
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing in Nehemiah 10:20, identifying a chief of the people who sealed the covenant renewal under Nehemiah. The name appears in a list of leaders publicly committing to Torah observance and separation from surrounding peoples. The LXX shows various Greek renderings, indicating the name was preserved in translation though its etymology is unclear. This individual was among the prominent leaders taking covenant responsibility.

senses.1: Magpiash, proper name of a leader in post-exilic Jerusalem. Nehemiah 10:20 lists him among chiefs of the people who sealed the covenant. The multilingual evidence shows transliteration (Magpias), preserving the Hebrew name. LXX variants (Bagaphes, Maiaphis, Megaias) show different Greek attempts at this Semitic name. His inclusion among covenant signatories marks him as a leader of restored Judah.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic verb meaning to overthrow or pull down, appearing in Ezra 6:12. The decree pronounces judgment on any king or people who would destroy the Jerusalem temple: 'May the God who has caused his name to dwell there overthrow any king or people.' This is Pael (intensive) form expressing forceful destruction. The verb emphasizes divine retribution against those who would harm God's sanctuary. The multilingual evidence shows this as violent overthrow or pulling down.

senses.1: Overthrow, pull down, destroy (divine action against temple destroyers). Ezra 6:12 invokes divine judgment: 'May He overthrow any king who alters this or destroys the temple.' This Aramaic Pael form indicates intensive action. The Spanish 'derribe' (knock down, overthrow) captures the violent reversal. The context of protecting God's house makes this about divine vengeance ensuring the temple's security against hostile powers.

gloss_terse: ledges, recesses, rebatements in temple walls
gloss_readable: A plural noun meaning ledges or recesses, appearing in 1 Kings 6:6 describing Solomon's temple construction. These were architectural features—indentations in the exterior temple walls that supported the beams of side chambers without requiring beams to be inserted into the holy wall itself. This clever design allowed attachment of auxiliary rooms while preserving the integrity of the main temple structure. The term emphasizes the technical architectural planning involved.

senses.1: Ledges, recesses, or rebatements in temple walls for supporting side chambers. 1 Kings 6:6 explains that Solomon made ledges around the temple exterior so beams wouldn't penetrate the sacred walls. The multilingual evidence (ledges, rebajos) captures this architectural feature. These stepped recesses allowed progressively narrower side chambers at each level while maintaining structural support without violating the temple's holy walls.

gloss_readable: A word of uncertain meaning in Joel 1:17, describing agricultural devastation. The MT reads 'the seed shrivels under their clods,' taking this as clods of earth. BDB notes Jewish interpreters favored 'clods,' while the LXX suggests a different reading (cribs or storehouses). Another proposal is 'shovels' from the agricultural context. The exact meaning remains debated, but the context is clearly one of drought and failed crops.

senses.1: Clods of earth, or possibly shovels (meaning disputed). Joel 1:17 describes agricultural ruin: seeds shrivel 'under their clods/shovels.' BDB presents multiple options: clods (following Jewish tradition and AV/RV), cribs (following LXX), or shovels (from Arabic cognate). The Spanish 'terrones-de-ellos' (their clods) follows the traditional reading. Despite lexical uncertainty, the image is agricultural desolation—whether dry clods, empty cribs, or unused tools.

gloss_readable: The Aramaic word for altar, appearing in Ezra 7:17 with the emphatic state. The Persian king's decree authorized using treasury funds to buy animals for sacrifice 'upon the altar of the house of your God which is in Jerusalem.' This Aramaic term is cognate with Hebrew 'mizbeach' and refers to the bronze altar of burnt offering in the temple courtyard where sacrifices were offered. The emphatic state ('the altar') specifies the particular altar at Jerusalem.

senses.1: The altar, specifically the altar of burnt offering in Jerusalem's temple. Ezra 7:17 uses this in the Aramaic portion of the king's decree funding temple sacrifices. The emphatic state marks this as the definite, specific altar at Jerusalem. The multilingual glosses (the-altar, el-altar) preserve the definiteness. This refers to the central structure where Israel's sacrificial worship was restored after exile.

gloss_readable: A poetic term for mouth as the organ of speech, appearing in Song of Solomon 4:3. The lover praises his beloved: 'Your mouth/speech is lovely,' parallel to 'your lips.' BDB distinguishes this from the common word for wilderness, identifying it as a separate root meaning mouth or speech. The LXX renders this 'lalia' (speech), and Jerome translates 'eloquium.' The term emphasizes the beauty of the beloved's words and manner of speaking.

senses.1: Mouth, speech, manner of speaking. Song of Solomon 4:3 uses this in love poetry: 'your speech is lovely,' in parallel with 'your lips are like scarlet thread.' The multilingual evidence (speech, habla, bouche) shows this as the speaking organ or speech itself. The LXX 'lalia' confirms this refers to speech or manner of speaking, not wilderness. The lover praises both the visual beauty of lips and the loveliness of words.

gloss_readable: A Piel perfect consecutive form of the verb 'to measure,' appearing in Job 7:4. Job complains, 'When I lie down I say, When shall I arise? But the night is prolonged/measured out.' Though from a root meaning 'measure,' here it carries the sense of being extended or prolonged—the night drags on interminably. Some versions render this 'the evening is measured out' emphasizing duration. Job's sleepless suffering makes nights feel endless.

senses.1: Measured out, prolonged, extended (of night's duration). Job 7:4 uses this in Job's lament: 'the night is prolonged/measured out' as he tosses sleeplessly. The Spanish 'Y-se-prolonga' (and it is prolonged) captures the sense of extension rather than literal measuring. Though the root means 'measure,' the context of sleepless suffering gives this the nuance of interminable duration—nights that seem to stretch on forever.

gloss_readable: A noun meaning tax or tribute, appearing in Nehemiah 5:4. This is a loanword from Assyrian 'mandattu' (tribute), ultimately from the root meaning 'to give.' The context is Jews borrowing money 'for the king's tax'—the Persian imperial levy imposed on the province. This financial burden, combined with drought and debt, created severe economic hardship for the returned exiles. The term emphasizes the obligatory nature of this payment to foreign overlords.

senses.1: Tax, tribute imposed by the Persian king. Nehemiah 5:4 records people borrowing money 'for the king's tax,' showing the economic strain of imperial levies on poor Jews. This loanword from Assyrian 'mandattu' indicates tribute or tax. The Spanish 'para-tributo-de' (for tribute of) captures the obligatory payment. The multilingual glosses (tax-of, tributo-de) emphasize this as revenue owed to Persian authorities, adding to the community's distress.

gloss_readable: A term in Isaiah 14:4 traditionally rendered 'golden city' but emended by most scholars to mean 'fury' or 'arrogance.' The MT reads 'madhebah' but LXX and most modern versions read 'marhebah' (fury, raging). The context is a taunt against Babylon's king: 'How the oppressor has ceased, the fury/arrogance ceased!' This emendation creates better parallelism with 'oppressor' and fits the pattern of denouncing Babylon's violent pride. The Spanish 'la-arrogancia' reflects this emended reading.

senses.1: Fury, arrogance, raging behavior (emended reading). Isaiah 14:4 in most modern versions reads: 'How the fury has ceased!' rather than MT's 'golden city.' BDB follows LXX and scholars reading 'marhebah' (boisterous rage) parallel to 'oppressor.' The Spanish 'la-arrogancia' (the arrogance) and context of denouncing Babylon's pride support this emendation. This describes Babylon's violent, raging oppression now ended.

gloss_readable: A plural noun meaning enticements or things that draw away, appearing in Lamentations 2:14. The prophets of Jerusalem 'saw for you false visions and enticements/banishments.' The term comes from a root meaning 'to thrust away' or 'lead astray,' suggesting deceptive prophecies that led the people away from truth. BDB connects this to the Hiphil sense of causing someone to turn aside. The context is prophetic deception contributing to Jerusalem's fall.

senses.1: Enticements, deceptive messages that lead astray. Lamentations 2:14 condemns false prophets who proclaimed 'visions of emptiness and enticements.' The root suggests thrusting away or drawing aside from the right path. The Spanish 'y-engaños' (and deceptions) captures the misleading nature. These prophetic messages enticed people away from repentance, contributing to the nation's blindness. The parallel terms 'vanity' and 'folly' reinforce the destructive deception.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic noun meaning dwelling or habitation, appearing in Daniel 2:11. In response to Nebuchadnezzar's impossible demand, the Chaldeans protest that 'there is no other who can declare it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with mortal flesh.' The term emphasizes the gods' separation from humanity—they dwell in a different realm. This highlights the impossibility of the request and sets up Daniel's revelation that the true God can reveal mysteries.

senses.1: Dwelling, habitation of the gods. Daniel 2:11 uses this in the Chaldeans' protest: the gods 'whose dwelling is not with flesh' cannot be consulted for such revelations. The Aramaic construct with suffix ('their dwelling') emphasizes divine transcendence—the gods live apart from humanity. The multilingual evidence (dwelling, morada, demeure) consistently renders this as habitation. This sets up the contrast with Daniel's God who does reveal mysteries despite dwelling separately.
